title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation scam in which fraudsters send personalized emails posing as Terry Gross and other Fresh Air staff to solicit fees from targets. The emails used plausible but unofficial addresses and were tailored to individual recipients, which made them more convincing than generic mass-fraud attempts. A cybersecurity expert cited in the reporting attributed this increased personalization to the use of artificial intelligence, though the specific tools or systems involved are not identified in the reporting.

The failure is not internal to a deployed AI product in the conventional sense. Instead, AI capabilities appear to have been applied outside any organizational guardrail, by actors using them to craft targeted deceptive messages at scale. There was no system within the scam pipeline designed to catch misuse, and the only friction came from recipients who noticed inconsistencies, such as a Gmail address or a payment request, rather than from any automated or institutional check.

What is not established is who the scammers are, which AI tools they used, or whether any specific AI provider bears responsibility. The reports describe ongoing investigations by WHYY, NPR, and Fresh Air, but no findings, charges, or attributions had been made at the time of publication.

reports.title: ‘Too good to be true?’: No, WHYY’s Terry Gross did not personally email you to be a guest on ‘Fresh Air’
Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

summary:
Scammers are impersonating Terry Gross and other staff members from the NPR show "Fresh Air" to defraud people. The fraudulent emails target authors, entertainers and other public figures with personalized messages about appearing on the show, but eventually ask recipients to pay fees, typically $250 for production costs. Professor Jennifer Black from Misericordia University received one such email and initially felt flattered, but grew suspicious when the message appeared to come directly from Gross herself and mentioned payment. Some emails came from addresses like "terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com."

WHYY, NPR and "Fresh Air" confirmed they are investigating these scams and stated they never charge guests for interviews or pay people for appearing on their programs. Cybersecurity expert Aunshul Rege explained that artificial intelligence has made impersonation scams more convincing and personalized than older mass-email fraud attempts. She advised people to verify requests through legitimate organizational contacts and to be suspicious of any request for payment or personal information. Similar scams have targeted other public figures including comedians Amy Poehler and Nikki Glaser, and journalist Katie Couric.
